name: Good faith (bona fides) in private law
plainSummary: Roman private law ties these ideas together: honesty, fair dealing, and faithfulness to agreements—so obligations and interpretation are guided by bona fides, not bare formalism alone.
description: Synthesis principle from classical Roman jurisprudence: obligations, interpretation, and conduct in private law should be guided by bona fides—honesty, fair dealing, and loyalty to the bargain—rather than compliance with the letter alone.
foundationStrengthRationale: Central to civilian systems and influential elsewhere; exact scope and institutional form vary by jurisdiction.

pros.claim: Aligns contract and property law with lived expectations of trust and cooperation.
pros.evidence: Good-faith standards appear across modern civil codes and influence common-law doctrines such as implied duties and unconscionability.

cons.claim: Open-ended good-faith language can create uncertainty about duties and liability.
cons.evidence: Debates over certainty vs. flexibility recur wherever courts imply obligations beyond express terms.

good-faith-uncertainty-note.title: Indeterminacy and good-faith standards — introductory note
